question: The idealised general circulation assumes:

options.text: An Earth with its axis tilted at 45° to its orbit
An all-land Earth with no oceans and a single uniform continent
That the sun is always overhead at 30°N, all year round
An all-sea Earth with the thermal and geographic equators coinciding

explanation: Removing land, surface variations and axial tilt leaves a simple pattern of pressure belts. The largely ocean-covered Southern Hemisphere comes closest to it.

question: The real general circulation differs from the idealised one mainly because of:

options.text: Small variations in the speed of the Earth's rotation through the year
Changes in the composition of the air from one latitude to another
Land–sea heating differences, varied surfaces and the 23½° axial tilt
The Moon's gravity acting on the atmosphere and the Earth's magnetic field

explanation: Continents heat and cool differently from the oceans, and the tilt makes the thermal equator move with the seasons.

question: In the idealised pattern, the subtropical high pressure belts lie at about:

options.text: 30°N and 30°S
60°N and 60°S
10°N and 10°S
45°N and 45°S

explanation: Air sinks at the poleward ends of the Hadley cells, around 30° latitude, forming the subtropical highs.

question: Surface air flowing from the subtropical highs towards the Equator forms the:

options.text: The polar easterlies, south-easterly in both hemispheres
The trade winds, north-easterly in the north and south-easterly in the south
The westerlies, blowing from the north-west in both hemispheres towards the Equator
The monsoon westerlies, south-westerly in both hemispheres

explanation: Coriolis deflection turns the equatorward flow to the right (north-east trades) in the north and to the left (south-east trades) in the south.

question: The four basic climatic zones in each hemisphere of the idealised pattern are:

options.text: Wet subtropical, dry equatorial, dry temperate and wet polar
Hot wet polar, cold dry equatorial, mild wet temperate and dry arid tropical at the Equator
Warm wet equatorial, warm arid subtropical, cool wet temperate and cold dry polar
Monsoon, desert, tundra and rainforest only

explanation: Rising air near the Equator and in the temperate lows brings rain; sinking air in the subtropical and polar highs brings dry weather.

question: The temperate-latitude westerlies blow between:

options.text: The trade wind belts, roughly 10–20°
The subtropical highs and the temperate lows, roughly 40–60°
The Equator and the subtropical highs, roughly 0–30° of latitude in each hemisphere
The poles and the temperate lows, roughly 60–90°

explanation: Poleward flow from the subtropical highs is turned by Coriolis to become westerly.

question: In the Southern Hemisphere, the strong westerlies between about 40° and 50°S are known as:

options.text: The Horse Latitudes
The Trades
The Doldrums
The Roaring Forties

explanation: With few land masses to interrupt them, the Southern Hemisphere westerlies are strong and persistent, with fast-moving depressions and frequent gales.

question: The "Horse Latitudes" are:

options.text: The light-wind areas under the subtropical highs, around 30–35°
The stormy westerlies of the Southern Ocean, found near 50°S (the "Roaring Forties")
The equatorial trough near the ITCZ, close to the Equator
The polar easterlies around the edges of the polar highs

explanation: Sailing ships could be becalmed for long periods under the subtropical highs.

question: As the north-east trade wind crosses the Equator into the Southern Hemisphere, it:

options.text: Keeps the same direction
Backs, becoming north-westerly
Reverses to become easterly
Veers, becoming south-easterly

explanation: South of the Equator the Coriolis deflection is to the left, so the wind turns anticlockwise (backs). The south-east trade veers to become south-westerly when it crosses northward.

question: Within the trade wind belts, weather is typically:

options.text: Fine on the poleward and eastern sides, more showery to the west and near the Equator
Uniformly stormy everywhere, with frequent tropical revolving storms
Foggy throughout the year, because of the cold ocean currents
Showery on the eastern sides of the oceans, and generally fine and dry on the western sides

explanation: On the eastern sides the trades are stable under the subsidence inversion. Towards the west and the Equator they have travelled further over warm water and become unstable.

question: In the Köppen classification, a tropical rain climate (class A) has:

options.text: A warmest month averaging below 10°C
Cold winters with months below −3°C
A coldest month above 18°C and no dry season
Evaporation that always exceeds precipitation

explanation: Class A is found roughly from 0° to 10°, the equatorial regions with rain in all seasons.

question: The Köppen dry climate (class B), such as the Sahara, is found roughly between:

options.text: 0–10° latitude, where rain falls all year
70° latitude to the poles, under the polar highs
50–70° latitude, with long snowy winters
20–35° latitude, where evaporation exceeds rainfall

explanation: These are the arid subtropical belts beneath the subtropical highs.

question: North-west Europe has which Köppen climate type?

options.text: Class B, dry (arid)
Class C, mid-latitude (warm temperate)
Class A, tropical rain climate with no cool season
Class E, snow (polar)

explanation: Class C covers the mid-latitudes with distinct summer and winter seasons but no prolonged severe cold.

question: The sub-arctic (snowy forest) climate, class D, of northern Eurasia and Canada has:

options.text: A coldest month above 18°C and no dry season at any time of year
No winter season, with rain in every month
A warmest month below 10°C throughout the year
A warmest month above 10°C and a coldest below −3°C

explanation: Long, cold winters and short summers characterise the boreal forests.

question: The Köppen snow (polar) climate, class E, has:

options.text: A coldest month above 18°C
Two rainy seasons
A warmest month averaging below 10°C
A Mediterranean pattern of dry summers

explanation: Areas such as north Greenland and Antarctica never have a month warm enough for trees.

question: The Mediterranean (temperate transitional) climate, around 35–40°, is characterised by:

options.text: Warm dry summers and cool wet winters
Rain throughout the year
Warm wet summers and warm dry winters
Very cold dry winters

explanation: In summer the subtropical high moves poleward over these regions; in winter the westerlies and depressions bring rain.

question: The tropical transitional (savannah) climate, around 10–20°, is characterised by:

options.text: Rain only at the equinoxes
Cold dry conditions all year
Warm wet summers and warm dry winters
Warm dry summers and cool wet winters

explanation: The ITCZ brings rain as it moves into these regions in summer; in winter the dry trade winds return.

question: Near the Equator, rainfall is greatest:

options.text: Around the equinoxes, when the thermal equator passes overhead
Only in January, during the southern summer monsoon
Only in July, during the northern summer monsoon
Around the solstices, when the sun is furthest from the Equator

explanation: The ITCZ crosses the equatorial belt twice a year, giving maxima around March and September.

question: Because of the tilt of the Earth's axis, the sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer (23½°N) on about:

options.text: 21 March
21 June
21 December
21 September

explanation: At the June solstice the sun is overhead at 23½°N; at the December solstice at 23½°S; at the equinoxes over the Equator.

question: North of the Arctic Circle (66½°N), on 21 June, the sun:

options.text: Stays below the horizon for 24 hours
Rises and sets exactly at 0600 and 1800
Is overhead at noon
Stays above the horizon for 24 hours

explanation: On the June solstice everywhere north of the Arctic Circle has continuous daylight. On 21 December it has continuous darkness.

question: In January, central Asia is exceptionally cold mainly because of:

options.text: Strong winds from the Indian Ocean crossing the Himalayas
Its position close to the Equator under the ITCZ
The warm Gulf Stream, which brings cold maritime Atlantic air in from the west over Siberia
Distance from the sea, long nights and constant radiative cooling over snow

explanation: Far from oceanic influence, the interior loses heat throughout the long winter, building the Siberian high.

question: Western Europe is milder in winter than other places at the same latitude mainly because:

options.text: It has no mountains to block the warm air from the south
The westerlies bring air warmed by the North Atlantic and the Gulf Stream
It lies slightly closer to the sun than other places at that latitude
Easterly winds from Siberia bring it warm continental air

explanation: The relatively warm ocean surface and the warm current keep the maritime air mild.

question: In July, compared with the Atlantic at the same latitude, central North America and Asia are:

options.text: Warmer, so the January pattern of isotherms is reversed
Colder, just as they are in January, because land loses heat quickly
Colder by about 20°C than the Atlantic
At the same temperature as the ocean

explanation: Land heats quickly in summer, so the continents become warmer than the oceans.

question: The annual range of temperature is greatest:

options.text: On small tropical islands, far from any continent
Over the equatorial oceans, where the sun is strongest all year
In the interiors of large high-latitude continents, such as Siberia
Over the Southern Ocean, in the westerly belt

explanation: Continental interiors heat strongly in summer and cool strongly in winter, while the sea moderates temperatures near the coast.

question: At the Equator, the freezing level is typically around:
explanation: The deep warm tropical troposphere puts the 0°C level high; hail from tropical storms often melts before reaching the ground.

question: Two-thirds of the world's land lies in the Northern Hemisphere. As a result:

options.text: The Northern Hemisphere follows the idealised circulation more closely
The Southern Hemisphere has larger seasonal swings in pressure
Seasonal land temperatures control pressure there far more than in the south
There are no subtropical highs anywhere in the Northern Hemisphere

explanation: The big northern continents create winter highs and summer lows that disrupt the ideal belts.

question: In January, the major semi-permanent pressure features of the Northern Hemisphere include:

options.text: A single deep low covering the whole of the Northern Hemisphere
The Icelandic and Aleutian lows and the Siberian, Azores and North American highs
The Baluchistan low over Pakistan and a large thermal low over central North America in winter
An Azores low and an Icelandic high, with the ITCZ over the Sahara

explanation: Winter cooling builds continental highs; strong winter depressions create the statistical lows near Iceland and the Aleutians.

question: In January, the equatorial low pressure trough lies:

options.text: South of the Equator over much of its length
Exactly on the Equator everywhere
Over Siberia, with the cold high to its south
North of the Equator, at about 20°N

explanation: The thermal equator follows the sun into the Southern Hemisphere in the southern summer, especially over the continents.

question: In July, the Siberian high is replaced by:

options.text: A col lying over Mongolia
A subtropical high centred over India
A large thermal low centred near Pakistan (the Baluchistan low)
An even stronger and colder anticyclone, centred over Siberia and northern Mongolia

explanation: Summer heating of the Asian landmass creates a vast area of low pressure that drives the south-west monsoon.

question: In July, the North Atlantic is dominated by:

options.text: The Azores high at its strongest, with a weak, split Icelandic low
A deep Icelandic low and a weak, broken Azores high further south
The ITCZ, which moves north to about 40°N
The Siberian high, extending westwards across Europe

explanation: The subtropical high strengthens and moves north in summer; the Icelandic low weakens.

question: The Icelandic low and the Aleutian low are described as "statistical lows" because:

options.text: They only appear on charts of statistics, not on real weather charts
They are thermal lows formed by heating of the land in summer
They are permanent features that never move from their positions
They result from averaging many passing depressions, not one permanent low

explanation: The frequent passage of deep depressions produces low average pressure, strongest in winter.

question: A monsoon is:

options.text: A daily alternation between land and sea breezes along a tropical coast, strongest in summer
A seasonal wind reversal caused by winter highs or summer lows over a continent
A cold katabatic wind blowing down from the Himalayas
A tropical revolving storm that crosses India each summer

explanation: Monsoons are most marked over South and South-East Asia, with a smaller system in West Africa.

question: The north-east monsoon over central India and Bangladesh in winter typically gives:

options.text: Tropical revolving storms daily
Persistent fog
Heavy rain and thunderstorms everywhere
Cool, dry, mainly clear weather

explanation: The air comes from the cold, dry Siberian high over land, so it carries little moisture.

question: The north-east monsoon brings heavy rain to south-east India and Sri Lanka because:

options.text: It comes directly down from the Himalayas
It picks up moisture over the Bay of Bengal first
It brings tropical revolving storms every day
It is a cold katabatic wind from the hills

explanation: A sea track adds moisture, giving cumulonimbus and heavy rain where the air meets the coasts and coastal mountains.

question: The south-west monsoon of India is produced by:

options.text: The south-east trades crossing the Equator and veering towards the Asian low
The north-east trades backing over the Arabian Sea and blowing away from the Asian low
The polar front moving south across India in summer
Cold air flowing south from Siberia across the Himalayas

explanation: Its long sea track makes it very moist, giving heavy cumulus, cumulonimbus and widespread thunderstorms from about June to September.

question: For flying, the south-west monsoon is generally:

options.text: Less hazardous than the north-east monsoon, with mainly light winds and little cloud
Hazardous only because of the dust it carries from Africa
More hazardous than the north-east monsoon, with storms, low cloud and turbulence
Free of cloud, because the air has crossed the dry Arabian desert

explanation: The very moist, unstable air produces deep convection and widespread poor weather.

question: The north-west monsoon of northern Australia and New Guinea is:

options.text: The north-east monsoon, backing as it crosses the Equator
A katabatic wind from the Great Dividing Range
A cold, dry wind blowing up from Antarctica
The south-east trades, backing over northern Australia

explanation: Having crossed warm seas, it brings cumulus, cumulonimbus and thunderstorms to northern Australia in the southern summer.

question: The ITCZ is caused mainly by:

options.text: Mountain barriers that lift the air
Convergence of the two trade wind systems near the thermal equator
Subsidence of air in the subtropical highs
Air masses of very different temperature meeting along a front

explanation: Unlike the polar front, the ITCZ separates air of similar temperature. Its cloud is produced by convergence and heating.

question: The width of the ITCZ can vary from about:

options.text: 1000 nm to 3000 nm
It is always exactly 50 nm
1 nm to 5 nm
25 nm to 300 nm

explanation: It is a broad, ill-defined zone rather than a sharp front.

question: Typical weather in an active ITCZ is:

options.text: Extensive cirrus only, with no cloud below about 30 000 ft
Fog and drizzle from low stratus, with no convective cloud
Cumulus and cumulonimbus, thunderstorms, turbulence and icing above about 16 000 ft
Clear skies, light winds and excellent visibility at all levels throughout the year

explanation: Cloud tops often reach 50 000 ft or more. In stable conditions the ITCZ may instead produce sheets of altostratus and nimbostratus.

question: Compared with the polar front, the ITCZ:

options.text: Is a sharp front with a large temperature contrast across it, like the polar front
Is found in the temperate latitudes, along with the polar front
Moves from west to east with the depressions forming on it
Has no sharp frontal surface, as the converging air is of similar temperature

explanation: Weather in the ITCZ comes from convergence and convection, not from warm air rising over cold air.

question: The seasonal movement of the ITCZ is:

options.text: Large over land and much smaller over the oceans
Zero; it is fixed on the Equator
The same everywhere, about 5° of latitude
Large over the oceans and much smaller over the continents

explanation: Land heats and cools more, so the thermal equator follows the sun further over the continents, for example into India and southern Asia in July.

question: In the eastern Mediterranean in winter, the subtropical jet near 200 hPa can produce:

options.text: Calm conditions
A tropical easterly jet
Westerlies often over 100 kt
Easterlies of about 50 kt, from the tropical jet

explanation: The subtropical jet often lies near Cyprus and the Egyptian coast in winter, sometimes exceeding 200 kt.

question: With the onset of the south-west monsoon over India, the high-level winds at 200 hPa:

options.text: Become northerly, flowing out from the Tibetan plateau
Become easterly as the subtropical jet moves north of the Himalayas
Become strongly westerly as the subtropical jet moves south of the Himalayas and over India
Become calm, as the monsoon low fills the whole troposphere

explanation: The tropical easterly jet replaces the winter westerlies over India in summer.

question: Upper winds over the polar regions in winter are generally:

options.text: Calm, as there is no pressure gradient over the pole
Northerly, flowing out from the polar high at all levels
Westerly, as the polar tropopause is colder than the temperate one
Easterly, as the poles are colder than the mid-latitudes at all levels

explanation: Cold polar air aloft makes a thermal wind that is westerly. In summer the polar tropopause becomes warmer than further south and the winds can turn easterly.

question: An easterly wave is:

options.text: A westward-moving trough in the trade winds, starting over West Africa
A warm front moving eastward in the westerlies of the mid-latitudes
A sea breeze front moving inland along a tropical coast
A jet stream feature found over the poles in winter

explanation: Easterly waves bring bands of showers and thunderstorms and may develop into tropical revolving storms.

question: In the Southern Hemisphere, polar front depressions:

options.text: Move from east to west
Only occur in December and January, during the southern summer
Form mostly at about 20°S
Centre on about 50°S throughout the year

explanation: The Southern Ocean has few land masses, so the polar front zone is fairly constant, affecting the south of South America, New Zealand and southern Australia.

question: Outbreaks of very cold polar air in winter behind cold fronts are particularly marked over:

options.text: The Southern Ocean and New Zealand
Central and northern China, and the central and southern USA
Western Europe and the British Isles
The Amazon basin and the central plains of Brazil, south to Argentina

explanation: Open terrain to the north lets polar continental air sweep south, bringing temperatures far below the average for those latitudes.

question: The world's heaviest rainfall is produced mainly by:

options.text: Cold continental anticyclones
The ITCZ and the monsoons
The polar highs
The subtropical highs

explanation: Rising air in the tropics and monsoon regions gives the largest totals. The subtropical and polar highs are dry.

question: Close to the South Pole, the surface winds are typically:

options.text: Light westerlies, from the temperate depressions far to the north
Calm all year, under the polar high
Strong westerlies, from the polar night jet
Strong easterlies, from polar outflow turned to the left

explanation: Air flowing out from the Antarctic high is deflected left in the Southern Hemisphere, producing easterlies, often reinforced by katabatic drainage.

question: Over the oceans, the surface pressure pattern keeps close to the idealised belts, but over the continents it:

options.text: Remains exactly as in the idealised belts throughout the year
Shows no pressure systems at all
Changes with the seasons, giving winter highs and summer lows
Shows permanent low pressure all year round

explanation: Land heats and cools far more than the sea, reversing the pressure pattern seasonally.

question: The trade winds blow most steadily:

options.text: Over the eastern parts of the tropical oceans
In the westerly belt near 50°
Near the poles in winter
Over large continents in summer, when heating is strongest

explanation: Over the open ocean, away from continental heating, the trades are remarkably constant in direction and speed.

question: The doldrums are:

options.text: The calm air beneath the polar highs
The light, variable winds of the equatorial trough
The steady trade winds of the tropics, blowing towards the ITCZ
The strong westerlies of the Southern Ocean

explanation: Converging trade winds near the Equator rise rather than blow horizontally, leaving light and variable surface winds with showers.

question: In January, the mean surface wind over India and Bangladesh is:

options.text: Southerly
South-westerly
Westerly
North-easterly

explanation: In winter the north-east monsoon blows from the Asian high.

question: In July, the mean surface wind over India is:

options.text: South-westerly
North-easterly
Easterly
Northerly

explanation: The south-west monsoon flows into the Asian summer low.

question: Over northern Australia in January, the mean surface wind is:

options.text: South-easterly trade
Calm
North-westerly monsoon
Strong westerly

explanation: The north-east monsoon from Asia backs as it crosses the Equator.
